Subject: Billing question: embeddings + generation across long chat history

Hi Karthik —

We're evaluating Redwood for our customer support assistant and have a few scenarios that are unclear on billing:

1) A single user session with a 12k token rolling context (past messages) where we call embeddings for reranking and then generate a summary for the agent. Are we billed for the full 12k context each request, or is there any aggregation/windowing?

2) If a lot of the context is cold (cached KV), how does that affect chargeable context?

3) Do you round small generation requests to a minimum billing increment? Our experiments show many short answers (~6–20 tokens) — curious how these get priced to estimate unit economics.

I've attached a tiny sample of our usage pattern (acme_usage_pattern.csv) to illustrate request cadence. Can you outline a few concrete examples for cost modeling?

Thanks —

From: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai

Hi Jessica — thanks for the sample, that's helpful. High level answers first, then a couple of worked examples using your CSV.

Summary bullets:
- Context tokens: billed on a per-conversation-rollup basis inside a 60-second roll-up window. If multiple requests arrive within the same conversation id inside that window, we only charge once for the shared prefix/context; subsequent requests are charged for novel input tokens and the output tokens.
- KV/cache: cached prefix tokens are billed at a discounted rate (we bill cache hits at 10% of normal input token cost) because they avoid recomputation; cache misses are billed at full input rate.
- Generation rounding: generation + input tokens are summed per request and rounded up to the nearest 4-token increment for billing (we use 4-token quantum to keep metering stable for micro-responses). There is no arbitrary 16-token minimum per request; instead we apply the 4-token quantum and a monthly minimum spend floor can be negotiated.

Worked example (using your pattern):
- Case A: Single request, 12,000 token context, 40 token user query, 80 token generated response. If the request is the only activity in that conversation in the 60s window, we charge: 12,000 context tokens (input) + 40 input + 80 output = 12,120 tokens (rounded to nearest 4 -> 12,120). If a second request arrives 25s later in same conversation that reuses a 11,900 token prefix (cached), and asks for a 30 token response, billing would be: novel input tokens (100) + 30 output = 130 -> rounded to 132 tokens; cached prefix billed at 10% of the per-token input rate (11,900 * 10%).
- Case B: Frequent short answers (many 6–20 token responses) within a chat session: each request still gets rounded to 4-token quantum; but with roll-up the shared context is amortized across requests in the 60s window so per-response cost drops materially.

Attachments: I exported a short CSV with the above calculations (billing_examples_acme.csv).

If helpful, I can jump on a 30-min call with our pricing ops to walk through larger monthly volumes and show model-by-model deltas.

Best,
Karthik Iyer
Head of GTM Pricing
Redwood Inference

Looping in a commercial note from our side. Jessica — great questions. A couple of commercial guardrails for modeling: 

- For new enterprise customers we typically offer a step-down on context token list price beyond a monthly threshold. For Acme we can propose: 20% list discount on context tokens above 100M tokens/month. Generation tokens (output) remain at standard list unless we include a bundled bundle.
- Round-up quantum (4 tokens) and the 60s conversation roll-up are our current billing mechanics; we can make roll-up window configurable in Dedicated/Private deployments but hosted customers use the default 60s.
- Retroactivity: discounts apply starting on the SOW effective date; we do not retroactively apply to prior invoices.

Next steps: if you're happy with the mechanics above, I'll ask Sales Ops to prepare an SOW draft and propose the discount bands. Ben — can you draft SOW v1 with the 20% tier for context tokens and include the 60s roll-up language?

Thanks,
Marissa Cole
